intro.text: Seven pages for the prophets of Israel’s first centuries, from the call at the bush to Samuel’s old age: Moses, his brother Aaron and sister Miriam, Eldad and Medad in the camp, Balaam son of Beor, Deborah, and Samuel.
Later Scripture looks back on this age as led by prophets: "by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet was he preserved", and "I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam."
The law of Moses gives Israel a test for a word spoken in the LORD’s name: "if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken".
When Samuel was a child "the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision". Peter later counts "all the prophets from Samuel and those that follow after".

Moses, Deborah and Samuel also led Israel, and their ruler pages tell that story. These pages are about the word alone: how it came, what was said and to whom, and what Scripture itself says came of it.

prophets.name: Moses
prophets.title: Prophet with whom the LORD spoke "mouth to mouth" (Numbers 12:8)
prophets.tagline: Sent from the bush to Pharaoh; Scripture says no prophet arose in Israel like him.

claim.text: Moses and Aaron brought Pharaoh the LORD’s word, "Let my people go", and Pharaoh answered, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice to let Israel go?" After the darkness Pharaoh told Moses he would die the day he saw his face again, and Moses answered, "Thou hast spoken well, I will see thy face again no more."

quote.text: Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Let my people go, that they may hold a feast unto me in the wilderness.
God called unto him out of the midst of the bush, and said, Moses, Moses. And he said, Here am I.

claim.text: While Moses kept Jethro’s flock at Horeb, the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a bush that burned and was not consumed. God named himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and sent him: "I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people".

call.label: Exodus 3–4 · Questions, signs and a mouth

quote.text: Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say.

claim.text: Moses asked "Who am I", asked God’s name and was told "I AM THAT I AM", said the people would not believe him, and said he was "slow of speech". God gave him three signs, promised to be with his mouth, and, when Moses still asked to be excused, gave him Aaron as spokesman.

quote.text: I am the LORD: speak thou unto Pharaoh king of Egypt all that I say unto thee.

claim.text: In Egypt the LORD sent Moses to Pharaoh again. Moses answered that he was "of uncircumcised lips"; the LORD said, "See, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh: and Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet."

quote.text: And now come, I will send thee into Egypt.

claim.text: Stephen tells the call as happening "when forty years were expired", in "the wilderness of mount Sina", where Exodus says Horeb. He gives the words from the bush and the sending in his own order.

how.text: Exodus says "the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend", and Deuteronomy closes with a prophet "whom the LORD knew face to face".

When Aaron and Miriam asked whether the LORD had spoken only by Moses, the LORD answered that he makes himself known to a prophet "in a vision" and speaks to him "in a dream", but with Moses "mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches".
At the tabernacle the LORD promised to speak with Moses "from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims", and Numbers says Moses heard the voice there.

At Sinai the people asked Moses, "Speak thou with us, and we will hear: but let not God speak with us". Moses later said he "stood between the LORD and you at that time, to shew you the word of the LORD".

Our count in the KJV: "the LORD spake unto Moses" stands in 105 verses (Exodus 20, Leviticus 33, Numbers 51, Deuteronomy 1) and "the LORD said unto Moses" in 55 (Exodus 36, Leviticus 2, Numbers 13, Deuteronomy 2, Joshua 2). The phrase "the word of the LORD came", used of later prophets such as Elijah, is never used of Moses.

The LORD told Moses to write a memorial against Amalek and the words of the covenant; Scripture says Moses wrote "all the words of the LORD", the stages of the journey, "this law", and a song taught to Israel.

He sang: the song at the sea, "Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the LORD", and the song he spoke "in the ears of all the congregation" before his death. Revelation speaks of "the song of Moses the servant of God".

message.theme: The God who sends

claim.text: At the bush God gave his name and told Moses what to say to Israel: the God of their fathers had seen their affliction and would bring them out to a good land.

quotes.text: I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.

message.theme: Let my people go

claim.text: The word to Pharaoh called Israel the LORD’s firstborn son and warned that if Pharaoh refused, his own firstborn would die.

quotes.text: Israel is my son, even my firstborn

message.theme: The covenant words

claim.text: Moses told the people "all the words of the LORD", wrote them, and read "the book of the covenant"; the people answered, "All that the LORD hath said will we do". In Deuteronomy he set the law before them again.

quotes.text: Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD: And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might.

message.theme: Blessing and curse set before them

claim.text: Deuteronomy sets out blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience, including scattering "among all people", and Moses calls heaven and earth to witness the choice.

quotes.text: I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live

message.theme: A prophet like Moses, and how to know a true word

claim.text: Moses told Israel not to listen to diviners and enchanters as the nations did, for the LORD would raise up a prophet "like unto me" and put his words in his mouth. A prophet who spoke presumptuously in the LORD’s name would die, and a word that did not come to pass was one "the LORD hath not spoken".

quotes.text: The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken
When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken

message.theme: The spirit shared

claim.text: When Joshua asked him to forbid Eldad and Medad from prophesying in the camp, Moses refused.

quotes.text: would God that all the LORD’s people were prophets, and that the LORD would put his spirit upon them!

quote.text: Thus saith the LORD, About midnight will I go out into the midst of Egypt: And all the firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die

claim.text: Moses went out from Pharaoh "in a great anger" after giving this word.

quote.text: Hereby ye shall know that the LORD hath sent me to do all these works; for I have not done them of mine own mind.

claim.text: Moses said that if the men died a common death, "then the LORD hath not sent me"; but if the earth swallowed them, the people would know these men had provoked the LORD.

quote.text: Enviest thou for my sake?
Hear now, ye rebels; must we fetch you water out of this rock?

claim.text: The LORD told Moses and Aaron they would not bring the congregation into the land, "because ye believed me not"; a psalm says Moses "spake unadvisedly with his lips".

quote.text: Happy art thou, O Israel: who is like unto thee, O people saved by the LORD

claim.text: Deuteronomy 33 is "the blessing, wherewith Moses the man of God blessed the children of Israel before his death", tribe by tribe.

signs.label: The rod, the hand and the water

claim.text: At the bush God gave Moses three signs "that they may believe": the rod that became a serpent, the hand made leprous and whole again, and river water that would become blood.

Deuteronomy says no prophet was like Moses "in all the signs and the wonders, which the LORD sent him to do in the land of Egypt"; Stephen speaks of "wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, and in the Red sea, and in the wilderness forty years".
Moses stretched out his hand over the sea and the LORD drove it back by a strong east wind; Israel crossed on dry ground and "believed the LORD, and his servant Moses".
At Horeb Moses struck the rock at the LORD’s word and water came out; at Meribah he struck the rock twice and the water "came out abundantly".
Coming down from Sinai with the tables, Moses "wist not that the skin of his face shone", and the people were afraid to come near him.

At the LORD’s word Moses set a serpent of brass on a pole, and whoever was bitten and looked at it lived. Jesus said, "as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up".

word.text: At the bush the LORD told Moses that the king of Egypt would not let Israel go, and that he would harden Pharaoh’s heart.

reported.text: Exodus says again and again that Pharaoh’s heart was hardened "as the LORD had said"; once "as the LORD had spoken unto Moses", and once "as the LORD had spoken by Moses".

word.text: Moses said the earth would open its mouth and swallow Korah’s company if the LORD had sent him.

reported.text: "It came to pass, as he had made an end of speaking all these words, that the ground clave asunder that was under them".

word.text: Moses promised that when Israel crossed the Jordan the LORD would give them "rest from all your enemies round about".

reported.text: At the temple Solomon said, "there hath not failed one word of all his good promise, which he promised by the hand of Moses his servant".

word.text: The law warned that if Israel would not hearken, "all these curses shall come upon thee", and the LORD would scatter them among all people.

reported.text: Daniel prays that "the curse is poured upon us, and the oath that is written in the law of Moses", and "As it is written in the law of Moses, all this evil is come upon us".

word.text: "The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me".

reported.text: In the temple Peter quotes the promise in his own wording ("him shall ye hear in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you"; "every soul, which will not hear that prophet, shall be destroyed from among the people"), and a few verses on says, "Unto you first God, having raised up his Son Jesus, sent him to bless you". Stephen quotes it too: "This is that Moses, which said unto the children of Israel, A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear." Stephen does not say in that verse who the prophet is.

word.text: Moses wrote the law and gave it to the priests and the elders.

reported.text: Jesus said, "had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me", and after the resurrection that "all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me".

claim.text: His brother, three years older by Exodus 7:7, given to him as spokesman: "he shall be to thee instead of a mouth, and thou shalt be to him instead of God".
His sister and Aaron’s, "the prophetess", who led the women’s song at the sea and later spoke against him with Aaron.
"His servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, departed not out of the tabernacle"; he asked Moses to forbid Eldad and Medad.
The priest of Midian, his father-in-law, whose flock he kept when he was called at the bush.
Two men who prophesied in the camp; Moses would not forbid them.
With Dathan and Abiram he gathered against Moses and Aaron: "Ye take too much upon you".
Exodus does not name Pharaoh’s magicians, who did "in like manner with their enchantments". 2 Timothy names two men who "withstood Moses", Jannes and Jambres, and says no more about them.

places.name: Horeb, the mountain of God, where he was called
Egypt, where he spoke to Pharaoh
Mount Sinai, where he received the law
The plains of Moab, where he gave the law again

scripture.text: The LORD told Moses he would see the land but not enter it, because at Meribah "ye sanctified me not in the midst of the children of Israel".

"So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD." He was 120, "his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated"; "he buried him in a valley" over against Beth-peor, "but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day".
Jude says the archangel Michael "disputed about the body of Moses" with the devil.
At the transfiguration Moses and Elias appeared and talked with Jesus; Luke says they "spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem".

tradition.text: Josephus, retelling Deuteronomy, says that as Moses was embracing Eleazar and Joshua "a cloud stood over him on the sudden, and he disappeared in a certain valley, although he wrote in the holy books that he died, which was done out of fear, lest they should venture to say that, because of his extraordinary virtue, he went to God."

Origen speaks of "the work entitled The Ascension of Moses (a little treatise, of which the Apostle Jude makes mention in his Epistle)", in which the archangel Michael disputes "with the devil regarding the body of Moses". The book is not part of Scripture.

questions.question: Who is the prophet "like unto me" of Deuteronomy 18:15–19?

views.label: The Messiah alone
views.holders: "The prevailing opinion in the early Church", revived by Kurtz, Auberlen and Tholuck, as reported by Keil (1871)

argument.text: Keil reports this as the early church’s main reading, which applied the promise directly and only to Christ, comparing Numbers 12:6–8, Deuteronomy 34:10 and Hebrews 3. Keil himself calls that use of those verses "unwarrantable".

views.label: The Old Testament prophets only
views.holders: von Hofmann, Baur and Knobel, as reported by Keil (1871)

argument.text: Keil reports that these scholars restrict the promise to the prophets of the Old Testament, "to the exclusion of the Messiah". He rejects the limit.

views.label: A line of prophets, with Christ included

argument.text: Both read "a prophet" as the prophets God would send whenever Israel needed a mediator, so that Israel need not turn to soothsayers. Keil adds that Christ, "in whom the prophetic character culminated", is included. Driver says the passage refers to "a prophetical order", and "may be reasonably understood as including" an ideal prophet in whom the line would culminate.

questions.question: Did Moses write the five books, and who wrote the account of his death?

views.label: Moses wrote them, apart from the last chapters

argument.text: Keil holds that "there is nothing in the whole of the five books which Moses might not have written", except "the last chapters of the fifth book", added "by a different hand" after Moses handed the finished book to the Levites (Deuteronomy 31:24). Of Deuteronomy 32:48–52 he says the account "was not written by Moses himself".

Driver concludes that Deuteronomy belongs "most probably, either to the reign of Manasseh, or to the early years of the reign of Josiah", in the 7th century BC, and that its author "builds upon the foundation of the prophets".

notSaid: Scripture names particular things Moses wrote (see "How the word came"), but the verses themselves do not say who wrote the five books as a whole.
Deuteronomy 34:6 says only "he buried him", and that "no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day".
John’s Gospel reports people asking about "that prophet" (John 1:21, 1:25; 6:14; 7:40), but does not cite Deuteronomy 18 at those places.
Exodus does not name the Pharaoh Moses faced, and Scripture gives no year BC for his call.

prophets.name: Aaron
prophets.title: Moses’ spokesman: "Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet" (Exodus 7:1)
prophets.tagline: Spoke the words the LORD gave Moses, to the elders of Israel and to Pharaoh.

claim.text: Aaron went in with Moses and told Pharaoh, "Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Let my people go". The king answered, "Wherefore do ye, Moses and Aaron, let the people from their works? get you unto your burdens."

quote.text: Aaron thy brother shall speak unto Pharaoh, that he send the children of Israel out of his land.

claim.text: Besides their joint speaking, Scripture records Aaron answering Moses. At the calf he said, "thou knowest the people, that they are set on mischief"; after Nadab and Abihu died he answered Moses about the sin offering; and after he and Miriam spoke against Moses he pleaded with him for her.

quote.text: Alas, my lord, I beseech thee, lay not the sin upon us, wherein we have done foolishly, and wherein we have sinned.
Is not Aaron the Levite thy brother? I know that he can speak well.

claim.text: When Moses asked to be excused, the LORD named Aaron as his spokesman to the people: "he shall be to thee instead of a mouth, and thou shalt be to him instead of God."

quote.text: And the LORD said to Aaron, Go into the wilderness to meet Moses.

claim.text: Aaron met Moses "in the mount of God". Moses told him all the words and signs; Aaron spoke the words to the elders of Israel and did the signs, "And the people believed".

quote.text: See, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh: and Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet.

claim.text: Moses was to speak all the LORD commanded, and Aaron was to speak it to Pharaoh.

how.text: The word came to Aaron through Moses: "thou shalt speak unto him, and put words in his mouth: and I will be with thy mouth, and with his mouth". "Aaron spake all the words which the LORD had spoken unto Moses".

Keil reads Exodus 4:16 and 7:1 together: "Aaron would stand in the same relation to Moses, as a prophet to God: the prophet only spoke what God inspired him with"; at 7:1 Aaron is "the prophet of Moses, as being the person who would announce to Pharaoh the revelations of Moses."
Our count in the KJV: the LORD speaks to Aaron alone in five places (Exodus 4:27; Leviticus 10:8; Numbers 18:1, 18:8, 18:20), and to Moses and Aaron together in 17 verses.

As high priest he was to bear the breastplate of judgment, with "the Urim and the Thummim", upon his heart before the LORD, and Moses put them in the breastplate; later his son Eleazar was to ask counsel "after the judgment of Urim".
Exodus 7:1 is the only verse that calls Aaron a prophet, and there he is the prophet of Moses.

message.theme: Let my people go

claim.text: With Moses he asked Pharaoh to let the people go three days’ journey into the desert to sacrifice to the LORD.

quotes.text: The God of the Hebrews hath met with us: let us go, we pray thee, three days’ journey into the desert, and sacrifice unto the LORD our God

message.theme: The blessing

claim.text: Through Moses the LORD gave Aaron and his sons the words with which they were to bless Israel: "And they shall put my name upon the children of Israel; and I will bless them."

quotes.text: The LORD bless thee, and keep thee: The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.

message.theme: Teaching the statutes

claim.text: The LORD told Aaron that the priests were to put difference between holy and unholy and to teach Israel the statutes given "by the hand of Moses".

quotes.text: that ye may teach the children of Israel all the statutes which the LORD hath spoken unto them by the hand of Moses

quote.text: And Aaron spake all the words which the LORD had spoken unto Moses, and did the signs in the sight of the people.

words.to: The people, at the golden calf

quote.text: To morrow is a feast to the LORD.

claim.text: When the people asked, "Up, make us gods", Aaron took their gold earrings and made a molten calf, built an altar before it, and proclaimed this feast. Exodus says the LORD plagued the people "because they made the calf, which Aaron made"; Moses says he prayed for Aaron, with whom the LORD "was very angry".

quote.text: Hath the LORD indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us?

claim.text: Aaron cast down his rod before Pharaoh and it became a serpent; the magicians did the same with their enchantments, "but Aaron’s rod swallowed up their rods".

At the LORD’s word through Moses, Aaron stretched out the rod over the waters, which became blood, then over the streams, and frogs came up, then struck the dust, which became lice. The magicians could not bring forth lice and said, "This is the finger of God".

signs.label: Between the dead and the living

claim.text: When a plague began after Korah’s rebellion, Aaron ran with a censer of incense into the congregation, "And he stood between the dead and the living; and the plague was stayed."

Twelve rods were laid before the LORD; Aaron’s rod "was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds", and was kept "for a token against the rebels". Hebrews lists it among the things in the ark.
His younger brother, for whom he spoke: "thou shalt be to him instead of God".
Exodus calls her "Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron"; she and Aaron spoke against Moses together, and Aaron pleaded for her when she was struck.
With Aaron he held up Moses’ hands at Rephidim; when Moses went up the mountain he told the elders, "Aaron and Hur are with you: if any man have any matters to do, let him come unto them."
His son, who received Aaron’s garments on mount Hor and ministered as priest after him.
Korah and his company gathered against Moses and Aaron; Moses asked them, "what is Aaron, that ye murmur against him?"

places.name: The mount of God, where he met Moses
Egypt, where he spoke to Pharaoh
Hazeroth, where he and Miriam spoke against Moses
Mount Hor, where Numbers says he died
Mosera, where Deuteronomy says he died
places.note: The atlas stores this place as Moseroth (Numbers 33:30); Deuteronomy 10:6 reads Mosera.

scripture.text: Because "ye rebelled against my word at the water of Meribah", Aaron was not to enter the land. On mount Hor Moses stripped him of his garments and put them on Eleazar, "and Aaron died there in the top of the mount"; Israel mourned him thirty days.
Numbers gives the date and age: he died "in the fortieth year" after the Exodus, "in the first day of the fifth month", aged 123.
Deuteronomy has a different place name: "to Mosera: there Aaron died, and there he was buried".
Later Scripture remembers him as "Aaron whom he had chosen" and "Aaron the saint of the LORD", and Hebrews says no man takes the priestly honour "but he that is called of God, as was Aaron".

tradition.text: Josephus, retelling Numbers, places Aaron’s death on a mountain by "a place which the Arabians esteem their metropolis, which was formerly called Arce, but has now the name of Petra", says he died "while the multitude looked upon him", in the same year as his sister, aged 123.

questions.question: Did Aaron die on mount Hor or at Mosera?

views.label: Both: Mosera was the camp below mount Hor

argument.text: Keil holds that the camp "is called Mosera in Deut. x. 6, and Moseroth" in Numbers 33, and lay in the Arabah near mount Hor, though "altogether unknown to us"; the camp took the mountain’s name because Aaron died and was buried there.

Driver notes that Numbers 33 lists the stations in another order and has Aaron die on mount Hor "not at Moserah". He thinks the difference is due to "divergent traditions", and that the itinerary in Deuteronomy 10 is likely "not part of the original text" of the book. He calls Keil’s reconciliation possible but not probable.

notSaid: Scripture records no prophecy of the future given through Aaron; his recorded words as a speaker are the words given to Moses.
Exodus does not record any word of the LORD to Aaron about the calf; Deuteronomy 9:20 says the LORD "was very angry with Aaron" and that Moses prayed for him.

prophets.name: Miriam
prophets.title: "Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron" (Exodus 15:20)
prophets.tagline: Led the women’s song at the sea; Micah names her with Moses and Aaron as sent before the people.

claim.text: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses "because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married" and asked whether the LORD had spoken only by him. The LORD answered for Moses, and Miriam became leprous; Moses cried to the LORD for her.

quote.text: Heal her now, O God, I beseech thee.

how.text: Exodus calls her "the prophetess" when she takes a timbrel and the women go out after her "with timbrels and with dances".
She and Aaron claimed that the LORD had spoken "also by us". The LORD’s answer said that to a prophet he makes himself known "in a vision" and speaks "in a dream", but with Moses "mouth to mouth".

Scripture names this Miriam in twelve verses (Exodus 15:20–21; Numbers 12:1, 4, 5, 10, 15; 20:1; 26:59; Deuteronomy 24:9; 1 Chronicles 6:3; Micah 6:4). The only words of hers it records are the refrain at the sea and the question she and Aaron asked in Numbers 12:2.

message.theme: The song at the sea

claim.text: After the crossing Moses and Israel sang. Miriam took a timbrel, the women went out after her, and she "answered them" with the opening words of the song.

quotes.text: Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea.

words.to: Those who sang at the sea

quote.text: And Miriam answered them, Sing ye to the LORD
Hath the LORD indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us?

claim.text: "And the LORD heard it."

When the cloud departed from the tabernacle, "Miriam became leprous, white as snow". At the LORD’s word she was shut out of the camp seven days, "and the people journeyed not till Miriam was brought in again". Deuteronomy later says, "Remember what the LORD thy God did unto Miriam by the way".
Her brother. Numbers and Chronicles name the three children of Amram and Jochebed: Aaron, Moses and Miriam.
Her brother, who spoke against Moses with her and pleaded for her: "Let her not be as one dead".
Josephus calls Hur "their sister Miriam's husband". Scripture does not say whom Miriam married.

places.name: The sea, where she led the women’s song
Kadesh in the desert of Zin, where she died and was buried

scripture.text: "The people abode in Kadesh; and Miriam died there, and was buried there."
Micah remembers her with her brothers as sent by the LORD: "I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam."

tradition.text: Josephus says Miriam died in the fortieth year after leaving Egypt, was given "a public funeral for her, at a great expense", and "was buried upon a certain mountain, which they call Sin", and that the people mourned her thirty days.

questions.question: Why is Miriam called "the prophetess" in Exodus 15:20?

views.label: For her gift of song and music

argument.text: Keil reports Rosenmüller’s view that the title was given "ob poeticam et musicam facultatem", that is, for her poetic and musical gift.

Keil holds she was called the prophetess "because of her prophetic gift", which, he says, "may serve to explain her subsequent opposition to Moses". He reads "the sister of Aaron" as marking her place beside Aaron, below Moses.

questions.question: Was Miriam the sister who watched the baby Moses (Exodus 2:4–8)?

argument.text: Josephus names her in his retelling: "Miriam, the child's sister, passed along upon the bank".
Keil calls Miriam Moses’ "deliverer in his infancy".
Exodus 2 says only "his sister" and "the maid". Numbers 26:59 and 1 Chronicles 6:3 name Miriam as the one sister of Aaron and Moses.

questions.question: Who was "the Ethiopian woman" of Numbers 12:1?

argument.text: Keil, who translates the Hebrew word as "Cushite", holds the wife "cannot have been Zipporah the Midianite", and that Moses had married a Cushite woman a short time before, "probably after the death of Zipporah".

views.label: Possibly Zipporah, if Cush means a north Arabian people

argument.text: Gray reports Winckler’s argument that "Cush" can name a north Arabian people; if so, the verse may be "a variant form of the tradition that Moses' wife was a Midianite". Gray says the verse in its present place "reasonably implies that the marriage was recent", and that "a decisive choice between these alternatives is scarcely justified."

views.label: An Ethiopian princess from Moses’ Egyptian years

argument.text: Josephus tells a story found nowhere in Scripture: as a general of Egypt, Moses married Tharbis, "the daughter of the king of the Ethiopians".

notSaid: Scripture gives no account of how the word first came to Miriam, and records no prophecy of hers about the future.
Exodus 15:20 calls her "the sister of Aaron"; Moses is not named in that verse.
Scripture does not say whom she married or whether she had children.
Numbers does not say why Miriam was struck and Aaron was not.

prophets.name: Eldad and Medad
prophets.title: Two men who "prophesied in the camp" (Numbers 11:26)
prophets.tagline: The spirit rested on them in the camp, and Moses would not forbid them.

claim.text: A young man ran to tell Moses, and Joshua asked him to forbid them. Moses refused.

quote.text: Enviest thou for my sake? would God that all the LORD’s people were prophets, and that the LORD would put his spirit upon them!

call.label: Numbers 11 · The spirit in the camp

quote.text: and the spirit rested upon them; and they were of them that were written, but went not out unto the tabernacle: and they prophesied in the camp.

claim.text: The LORD told Moses to gather seventy elders to the tabernacle, and took of the spirit that was on Moses and gave it to them. Two of the men, Eldad and Medad, had stayed in the camp, and the spirit rested on them there.

how.text: "The spirit rested upon them", the same words used of the seventy at the tabernacle.
Numbers says they "prophesied", but does not record anything they said.

claim.text: The spirit given to them was taken "of the spirit that was upon him".
"The servant of Moses, one of his young men", who said, "My lord Moses, forbid them."
Gathered round the tabernacle; when the spirit rested on them "they prophesied".

places.name: The camp at Kibroth-hattaavah
places.note: The chapter’s camp is named in verse 34; the text does not name the place of the elders’ gathering separately.

scripture.text: Scripture names them only in Numbers 11:26–27 and says nothing more of them.

questions.question: Were Eldad and Medad two of the seventy?

views.label: Yes, two of those chosen, who stayed in the camp
views.holders: Keil (1871); Gray says this is how the verse "is generally understood"

argument.text: Keil calls them "two of the persons who had been chosen", who "had remained behind in the camp, for some reason that is not reported".

views.label: Of the wider body of elders, not of the seventy

argument.text: Gray points out that verse 24 says the seventy went out to the tabernacle and verse 25 that the seventy received the spirit, and that Moses’ answer "implies that Eldad and Medad did not belong to the number". If the clause is original and not a later note, he says, it would be better to take "the registered" as "the whole body of elders from whom the seventy were chosen".

views.label: They went on prophesying
views.holders: The KJV ("and did not cease"), which Keil traces to the Vulgate and Onkelos

argument.text: Keil reports that the Vulgate and Onkelos render the clause "and ceased not". The KJV reads "they prophesied, and did not cease".

Keil renders "they prophesied, and did not add", that is, "they did not repeat the prophesyings any further", and calls the Greek rendering correct. Gray translates "They prophesied, but they did so no more".

questions.question: Was there a book of their prophecy?

argument.text: Numbers does not record their words.

views.label: A writing under their names was known in the 2nd century
views.holders: The Shepherd of Hermas (2nd century), in Lightfoot and Harmer (1891)

argument.text: The Shepherd of Hermas quotes it: "The Lord is nigh unto them that turn unto Him, as it is written in Eldad and Modat, who prophesied to the people in the wilderness." Lightfoot and Harmer call its date "uncertain" and say the book was in general circulation "soon after the middle of the second century".

notSaid: Scripture does not give their tribe or family, why they stayed in the camp, or what they said.
Nothing is said of them after Numbers 11:27.

prophets.name: Balaam
prophets.title: Son of Beor of Pethor; "the soothsayer" (Joshua 13:22) and "the prophet" (2 Peter 2:16)
prophets.tagline: Hired to curse Israel, he spoke only the word God put in his mouth, and blessed them.

claim.text: Balak sent elders of Moab and Midian "with the rewards of divination", then "princes, more, and more honourable", promising great honour. Each time Balaam would say only what the LORD gave him. After three blessings Balak said, "I called thee to curse mine enemies, and, behold, thou hast altogether blessed them these three times."

quote.text: If Balak would give me his house full of silver and gold, I cannot go beyond the word of the LORD my God, to do less or more.
Thou shalt not go with them; thou shalt not curse the people: for they are blessed.

claim.text: When Balak’s messengers came to Pethor, Balaam lodged them for the night, "and I will bring you word again, as the LORD shall speak unto me". God came to him and asked, "What men are these with thee?"

quote.text: If the men come to call thee, rise up, and go with them; but yet the word which I shall say unto thee, that shalt thou do.

claim.text: When the second embassy came, Balaam asked them to wait "that I may know what the LORD will say unto me more", and God came to him at night again.

call.label: Numbers 22 · The angel in the way

quote.text: Go with the men: but only the word that I shall speak unto thee, that thou shalt speak.

claim.text: "God’s anger was kindled because he went", and the angel of the LORD stood in the way. When his eyes were opened Balaam said, "I have sinned", and offered to go back; the angel sent him on with this charge.

how.text: "God came unto Balaam" by night; later "God met Balaam" and "the LORD put a word in Balaam’s mouth".

Twice, after Balak had built seven altars at his word and offered on them, Balaam went aside to meet the LORD. The third time "he went not, as at other times, to seek for enchantments", and "the spirit of God came upon him".

He calls himself "the man whose eyes are open", who "heard the words of God, and knew the knowledge of the most High, which saw the vision of the Almighty, falling into a trance, but having his eyes open".
The messengers brought "the rewards of divination"; Joshua calls him "the soothsayer"; 2 Peter calls him "the prophet".
The KJV of 2 Peter 2:15 calls his father "Bosor"; every other verse that names his father reads "Beor".
Josephus, retelling Numbers, calls Balaam "the greatest of the prophets at that time", and says he spoke "by inspiration, as not being in his own power".

message.theme: First parable: a people that dwells alone

claim.text: From the high places of Baal, where he could see the edge of the camp, Balaam said he could not curse those God had not cursed.

quotes.text: How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed? or how shall I defy, whom the LORD hath not defied?
Let me die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like his!

message.theme: Second parable: God is not a man

claim.text: From the top of Pisgah he said the blessing could not be reversed, and that "there is no enchantment against Jacob, neither is there any divination against Israel".

quotes.text: God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it?
Behold, I have received commandment to bless: and he hath blessed; and I cannot reverse it.

message.theme: Third parable: the tents of Jacob

claim.text: From the top of Peor, seeing Israel encamped by tribes, he blessed them under the spirit of God.

quotes.text: How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, and thy tabernacles, O Israel!
Blessed is he that blesseth thee, and cursed is he that curseth thee.

message.theme: Fourth parable: a Star out of Jacob

claim.text: Before going home he told Balak "what this people shall do to thy people in the latter days": a ruler from Israel would smite Moab and possess Edom.

quotes.text: I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel

message.theme: Last parables: Amalek, the Kenites, Asshur and Chittim

claim.text: He spoke of Amalek’s end, of the Kenites carried away by Asshur, and of ships from Chittim afflicting Asshur and Eber.

quotes.text: Alas, who shall live when God doeth this!

quote.text: the word that God putteth in my mouth, that shall I speak.
and shall smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth.
And Edom shall be a possession, Seir also shall be a possession for his enemies; and Israel shall do valiantly.
Amalek was the first of the nations; but his latter end shall be that he perish for ever.
Nevertheless the Kenite shall be wasted, until Asshur shall carry thee away captive.
And ships shall come from the coast of Chittim, and shall afflict Asshur, and shall afflict Eber, and he also shall perish for ever.

claim.text: Three times the ass saw the angel of the LORD with a drawn sword and turned aside, and Balaam struck her; "the LORD opened the mouth of the ass", and then "the LORD opened the eyes of Balaam". 2 Peter says "the dumb ass speaking with man’s voice forbad the madness of the prophet".
At Balaam’s word Balak built seven altars and offered a bullock and a ram on each, on the high places of Baal, in the field of Zophim on Pisgah, and on the top of Peor.
"Balak the son of Zippor was king of the Moabites at that time"; he sent for Balaam and took him to three heights to curse Israel.

person.name: The elders of Moab and Midian

claim.text: They came to Balaam "with the rewards of divination in their hand".
Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur and Reba, slain in the war on Midian; "Balaam also the son of Beor they slew with the sword".

places.name: The Arnon, where Balak met him
Bamoth-baal, the high places of Baal (first parable)
Pisgah and the field of Zophim (second parable)
The top of Peor (third and fourth parables)
Pergamos, where some held "the doctrine of Balaam"

scripture.text: "And Balaam rose up, and went and returned to his place: and Balak also went his way."
In the war on Midian, "Balaam also the son of Beor they slew with the sword". Joshua repeats it: "Balaam also the son of Beor, the soothsayer, did the children of Israel slay with the sword".
Moses says of the Midianite women, "these caused the children of Israel, through the counsel of Balaam, to commit trespass against the LORD in the matter of Peor".

Deuteronomy shuts Ammon and Moab out of the congregation partly "because they hired against thee Balaam the son of Beor of Pethor of Mesopotamia, to curse thee", and goes on, "Nevertheless the LORD thy God would not hearken unto Balaam; but the LORD thy God turned the curse into a blessing unto thee". Nehemiah reads the same law aloud: "howbeit our God turned the curse into a blessing".
Joshua gives the LORD’s words: Balak "sent and called Balaam the son of Beor to curse you: But I would not hearken unto Balaam; therefore he blessed you still".
Micah calls Israel to "remember now what Balak king of Moab consulted, and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him from Shittim unto Gilgal; that ye may know the righteousness of the LORD".

2 Peter speaks of "the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness"; Jude of those who "ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward"; Revelation of "the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balac to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel, to eat things sacrificed unto idols, and to commit fornication".

tradition.text: Josephus, retelling Numbers, gives Balaam’s counsel in full: on his way home, before crossing the Euphrates, he told Balak and the Midianites to send their most beautiful daughters to the Hebrew camp, so that the young men would leave their laws and worship the gods of Midian, "for by this means God will be angry at them".
Josephus adds that Moses did Balaam "great honor, by setting down his prophecies in writing", when he could have claimed them as his own.

questions.question: What was Balaam: a prophet of the LORD or a heathen soothsayer?

views.label: A sorcerer and false prophet, compelled by God
views.holders: Philo, Ambrose and Augustine, as reported by Keil (1871)

argument.text: Keil reports that these writers saw him as "a wizard and false prophet, devoted to the worship of idols", who was made "against his will" to bless instead of curse.

views.label: A true prophet who fell through covetousness
views.holders: Tertullian and Jerome, as reported by Keil (1871)

argument.text: Keil reports that these writers took him for "a genuine and true prophet, who simply fell through covetousness and ambition".

views.label: A soothsayer to whom God gave true words

argument.text: Keil holds that Balaam practised soothsaying "as a trade", yet knew and confessed the LORD, so that "without being really a prophet, he was able to give utterance to true prophecies from Jehovah". He points to "the soothsayer" in Joshua 13:22 and the enchantments of Numbers 24:1.

views.label: A figure of poetry more than of history

argument.text: Gray holds that "the story of Balaam as told in Numbers is largely poetic rather than historical"; the names Balaam and Balak "may have attached to historical individuals", but whether they belonged to the age of Moses "we are in no position to affirm".

questions.question: God told Balaam to go (22:20). Why was he angry "because he went" (22:22)?

views.label: Because of the way he went
views.holders: Keil (1871); Hengstenberg, as listed by Gray

argument.text: Keil holds that the anger was "not excited by the fact that Balaam went", but by his behaviour on the journey, as "a longing for wages and honour" filled his heart nearer his destination.

Gray holds that verse 22 is "not the original sequel" to verses 20–21, and that the story of the ass comes from a different source (J), in which Balaam set out without asking the LORD. He calls the other explanation a "harmonistic" one that "explains away the statement".

questions.question: Who is the "Star out of Jacob" (Numbers 24:17)?

views.label: A king of Israel: David
views.holders: Most non-Messianic interpreters, such as Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Dillmann, as listed by Gray (1903)

argument.text: Gray reports that most who read the verse of one person, but not of the Messiah, "have seen in the v. a reference to David's conquest of Moab" (2 Samuel 8:2); he adds that if verse 18 is original, "David, as the conqueror of both Moab and Edom", alone fits.

views.label: The Messiah, and the star of the magi

argument.text: Origen holds that the magi, "possessing as they did the prophecies of Balaam", found "the prophecy about the star" and concluded that the one foretold had come.

views.label: The Messiah: an old Jewish and Christian reading
views.holders: The Targums; Rabbi Akiba; Justin, Irenaeus and Cyprian onward, as reported by Gray (1903)

argument.text: Gray reports that a Messianic reading "was early attached to the words": the Targums give it, Akiba gave "the pseudo-Messiah in the time of Hadrian" the title "Bar-Kokba, son of the star", and from Justin, Irenaeus and Cyprian it "became general among Christian interpreters down to 1771". Gray himself holds that the words of the poem do not call for it.

views.label: Begun in David, completed in Christ

argument.text: Keil holds that the star and sceptre are a king "in the far distant future", and that the fulfilment "commenced with the subjugation of the Edomites by David" but "will not be completed till 'the end of the days'".

views.label: Pitru, near Carchemish by the Euphrates
views.holders: Generally accepted by 1903, Gray reports (e.g. Sayce, Schrader, Friedrich Delitzsch)

argument.text: Gray reports that the identification of Pethor with Pitru, named by Shalmaneser, "has been generally accepted"; Pitru lay "a little S. of Carchemish", on the Sajur near the Euphrates.
Keil holds that "the town of Pethor, or Pethora" is "unknown", and calls other proposed sites "very uncertain".

views.label: Somewhere near the "river of Egypt"
views.holders: Marquart and Cheyne, as reported by Gray (1903)

argument.text: Gray reports that some scholars questioned the Pitru identification on grounds of spelling and sought the place on the "river of Egypt"; to do so, he says, they explain away Deuteronomy 23:4 (23:5 in the Hebrew), which places Pethor in Mesopotamia.

notSaid: Numbers 25 tells of Israel at Peor without naming Balaam. Numbers 31:16 names him "in the matter of Peor"; Revelation 2:14 says he "taught Balac to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel", without naming Peor.
Numbers 24:25 says Balaam "returned to his place"; Scripture does not say how he came to be among the Midianites when he was killed (Numbers 31:8).
Matthew’s magi speak of "his star" (Matthew 2:2) but Matthew does not cite Numbers 24:17.
Kirjath-huzoth, where Balak feasted him (Numbers 22:39), is not in the site’s atlas.

prophets.name: Deborah
prophets.title: "A prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth", who judged Israel (Judges 4:4)
prophets.tagline: Gave Barak the LORD’s command and the day of battle, and sang the victory.

claim.text: Jabin, who reigned in Hazor, "mightily oppressed" Israel for twenty years. Scripture records no word between Deborah and Jabin; her word was about his captain Sisera.

quote.text: And I will draw unto thee to the river Kishon Sisera, the captain of Jabin’s army, with his chariots and his multitude; and I will deliver him into thine hand.

how.text: "She judged Israel at that time": she sat under the palm tree of Deborah between Ramah and Beth-el, "and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment".
She gave the LORD’s command to Barak as a question: "Hath not the LORD God of Israel commanded, saying, Go and draw toward mount Tabor".
The victory is told twice, in prose and in a song: "Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day". In the song she is called on: "Awake, awake, Deborah: awake, awake, utter a song".

message.theme: The LORD’s command to Barak

claim.text: Barak was to take ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun to mount Tabor, and the LORD would draw Sisera to the river Kishon and deliver him into his hand.

quotes.text: Hath not the LORD God of Israel commanded, saying, Go and draw toward mount Tabor, and take with thee ten thousand men of the children of Naphtali and of the children of Zebulun?

message.theme: The day of battle

claim.text: On the day itself she told Barak the LORD had already gone out before him.

quotes.text: Up; for this is the day in which the LORD hath delivered Sisera into thine hand: is not the LORD gone out before thee?

message.theme: The song: the LORD came from Seir

claim.text: The song praises the LORD for the people who "willingly offered themselves", recalls the LORD marching out of Seir and Edom, and remembers the days before Deborah arose "a mother in Israel".

quotes.text: LORD, when thou wentest out of Seir, when thou marchedst out of the field of Edom, the earth trembled, and the heavens dropped, the clouds also dropped water.
So let all thine enemies perish, O LORD: but let them that love him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his might.

message.theme: Those who came and those who stayed

claim.text: The song praises the tribes that came, among them Zebulun and Naphtali, who "jeoparded their lives unto the death". It asks why Reuben abode "among the sheepfolds" and why Dan remained "in ships", says Gilead and Asher stayed where they were, and gives a curse on Meroz from "the angel of the LORD".

quotes.text: Curse ye Meroz, said the angel of the LORD, curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof; because they came not to the help of the LORD

quote.text: I will surely go with thee: notwithstanding the journey that thou takest shall not be for thine honour; for the LORD shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman.

claim.text: Barak had said he would go only if she went with him.

quote.text: Up; for this is the day in which the LORD hath delivered Sisera into thine hand
Hear, O ye kings; give ear, O ye princes; I, even I, will sing unto the LORD
Curse ye Meroz, said the angel of the LORD, curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof

claim.text: The song gives the reason: "because they came not to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty".
The prose says "the LORD discomfited Sisera"; the song says "They fought from heaven; the stars in their courses fought against Sisera" and "The river of Kishon swept them away".
The son of Abinoam of Kedesh-naphtali, whom she called and went with; he sang the song with her. Hebrews 11:32 names Barak among the faithful.
Her husband, named only in Judges 4:4.
The wife of Heber the Kenite, who killed Sisera in her tent; the song calls her "Blessed above women".
Jabin’s captain, with nine hundred chariots of iron; he fled on foot and died in Jael’s tent.

places.name: The palm tree of Deborah, between Ramah and Beth-el
Harosheth of the Gentiles, Sisera’s city

scripture.text: Judges ends her story with the song and the words "And the land had rest forty years"; it does not record her death.

tradition.text: Josephus, retelling Judges, writes: "Now when Barak and Deborah were dead, whose deaths happened about the same time".

questions.question: Did Deborah make the song of Judges 5?

views.label: Yes
views.holders: Keil (1872); "the great majority of scholars", such as Ewald, Hitzig and Renan, as reported by Moore (1895)

argument.text: Keil holds that verse 1 means the song was sung by Deborah and Barak together, not made by both, and that "the poetess or writer of the song, according to vers. 3, 7, and 12, was Deborah."

views.label: A poet of the time, not Deborah
views.holders: Moore (1895); also Wellhausen, Reuss, Graetz, Kuenen and others, as listed by Moore

argument.text: Moore notes that some ancient versions read verse 7 in the third person, "until Deborah arose", and that the Hebrew "may equally well be rendered, until thou didst arise, Deborah"; verse 12 calls on her, and elsewhere the song speaks of her in the third person. He calls it "the natural and almost necessary inference" that "Deborah herself is not the author", and thinks it more probable "that the poem was made by one under the immediate inspiration of the events". He calls it "the oldest extant monument of Hebrew literature".

views.label: A late, artificial poem
views.holders: Maurice Vernes (1883–1892), as reported by Moore (1895)

argument.text: Moore reports that Vernes put the prose account no earlier than the 5th century BC and the song a century or more later, and called it an artificial work. Moore answers that Vernes’ facts, where accurate, "do not justify his conclusions".

notSaid: Judges gives no account of how the word first came to Deborah, and does not name her tribe.

Judges 4:9 says the LORD would sell Sisera "into the hand of a woman", and 4:21–22 tells how Jael killed him; the text sets the two side by side but does not say in so many words that the word came to pass.
Scripture does not record her death. Hebrews 11:32 names Barak, not Deborah.

prophets.name: Samuel
prophets.title: "Established to be a prophet of the LORD" (1 Samuel 3:20); also "the seer" (1 Samuel 9:19)
prophets.tagline: Called by name in the night at Shiloh; the LORD let none of his words fall to the ground.

claim.text: The first word recorded as given to Samuel was against Eli’s house. He was afraid to tell it, but Eli made him tell "every whit".

quote.text: It is the LORD: let him do what seemeth him good.

claim.text: Samuel anointed Saul and gave him signs; at Gilgal he told him "thy kingdom shall not continue"; after Amalek he told him the LORD had rejected him and rent the kingdom from him; and at Endor the one Saul called up as Samuel told him, "to morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me".

quote.text: Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.

claim.text: Sent to Jesse’s house, Samuel anointed the youngest son "in the midst of his brethren"; later David fled to Samuel at Ramah and they dwelt in Naioth.

quote.text: Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the midst of his brethren: and the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward.

claim.text: Samuel had Agag brought to him at Gilgal and "hewed Agag in pieces before the LORD".

quote.text: As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women.

call.label: 1 Samuel 3 · Called by name at Shiloh

quote.text: And the LORD came, and stood, and called as at other times, Samuel, Samuel. Then Samuel answered, Speak; for thy servant heareth.

claim.text: In days when "the word of the LORD was precious" and "there was no open vision", the LORD called the child as he lay down to sleep, before "the lamp of God went out". Three times he ran to Eli, until Eli "perceived that the LORD had called the child" and told him how to answer.

how.text: Before the call, "Samuel did not yet know the LORD, neither was the word of the LORD yet revealed unto him". Afterwards "the LORD revealed himself to Samuel in Shiloh by the word of the LORD. And the word of Samuel came to all Israel."
"The LORD had told Samuel in his ear a day before Saul came"; "Then came the word of the LORD unto Samuel"; at Jesse’s house the LORD named which son to anoint.
He was called "the seer": "he that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer". Saul’s servant said of him that everything he says comes to pass.
He prayed for the people: he "cried unto the LORD for Israel; and the LORD heard him", and promised, "God forbid that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you".
At Naioth in Ramah "the company of the prophets" prophesied with "Samuel standing as appointed over them".
He wrote: "Samuel told the people the manner of the kingdom, and wrote it in a book, and laid it up before the LORD." Chronicles cites "the book of Samuel the seer" for the acts of David.

message.theme: Return to the LORD with all your hearts

claim.text: At Mizpeh he called Israel to put away the strange gods and serve the LORD only, and promised deliverance from the Philistines.

quotes.text: If ye do return unto the LORD with all your hearts, then put away the strange gods and Ashtaroth from among you, and prepare your hearts unto the LORD, and serve him only

message.theme: The manner of the king

claim.text: When the elders asked for a king, the LORD told Samuel, "they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me", and Samuel warned them what a king would take from them.

quotes.text: And ye shall cry out in that day because of your king which ye shall have chosen you; and the LORD will not hear you in that day.

message.theme: Fear the LORD and serve him

claim.text: At Gilgal he recounted what the LORD had done from Moses on, and told the people that both they and their king must follow the LORD.

quotes.text: Only fear the LORD, and serve him in truth with all your heart: for consider how great things he hath done for you.

message.theme: To obey is better than sacrifice

claim.text: To Saul, who had kept the best of Amalek’s flocks "to sacrifice unto the LORD", Samuel answered that obedience counted for more than offerings.

quotes.text: For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, he hath also rejected thee from being king.

message.theme: Not as man seeth

claim.text: When Samuel looked at Eliab and thought him the LORD’s choice, the LORD corrected him.

quotes.text: for the Lord seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.

quote.text: Gather all Israel to Mizpeh, and I will pray for you unto the LORD.
I will call unto the LORD, and he shall send thunder and rain; that ye may perceive and see that your wickedness is great
But now thy kingdom shall not continue: the LORD hath sought him a man after his own heart
The LORD hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou.
The LORD hath not chosen these.
to morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me

claim.text: The words are spoken by the one the woman brought up and Saul "perceived" to be Samuel; see the open question.
As Samuel offered a lamb and cried to the LORD, "the LORD thundered with a great thunder on that day upon the Philistines, and discomfited them".

signs.label: Thunder and rain at wheat harvest

claim.text: At Gilgal Samuel called on the LORD at wheat harvest, "and the LORD sent thunder and rain that day: and all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel".

signs.label: Oil and three signs for Saul

claim.text: Samuel poured oil on Saul’s head and told him three things he would meet on the way home, ending with a company of prophets with whom he would prophesy.
When Saul caught the skirt of Samuel’s mantle and it tore, Samuel said the LORD had torn the kingdom from him that day.
Three companies of Saul’s messengers, and then Saul himself, prophesied when they came near Samuel and the prophets at Naioth: "Wherefore they say, Is Saul also among the prophets?"

word.text: Samuel told Saul what he would meet on the way: two men at Rachel’s sepulchre, three men going up to Beth-el, and a company of prophets.

reported.text: "And all those signs came to pass that day."

word.text: "I will call unto the LORD, and he shall send thunder and rain".

reported.text: "So Samuel called unto the LORD; and the LORD sent thunder and rain that day".

word.text: The LORD’s first word to Samuel: "In that day I will perform against Eli all things which I have spoken concerning his house". A man of God had already told Eli the same.

reported.text: When Solomon put Abiathar out of the priesthood, Kings says he did it "that he might fulfil the word of the LORD, which he spake concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh".

word.text: Samuel anointed David at the LORD’s word to be king in Saul’s place.

reported.text: At Hebron the elders "anointed David king over Israel, according to the word of the LORD by Samuel".

word.text: "The LORD hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine".

reported.text: At Endor the one Saul took for Samuel said: "the LORD hath done to him, as he spake by me: for the LORD hath rent the kingdom out of thine hand, and given it to thy neighbour, even to David".

word.text: Samuel told Eli the word "every whit", and "the word of Samuel came to all Israel".

reported.text: "The LORD was with him, and did let none of his words fall to the ground. And all Israel from Dan even to Beer-sheba knew that Samuel was established to be a prophet of the LORD."

claim.text: The priest at Shiloh, before whom "the child Samuel ministered unto the LORD", and who taught him to answer, "Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth".
The king he anointed and later rejected; "Samuel came no more to see Saul until the day of his death: nevertheless Samuel mourned for Saul".
The king he anointed; David fled to him at Ramah.
A company met Saul coming down from the high place with music, and at Naioth they prophesied with Samuel "standing as appointed over them".

scripture.text: "And Samuel died; and all the Israelites were gathered together, and lamented him, and buried him in his house at Ramah."

1 Samuel 28 tells of the woman at Endor bringing up one whom Saul "perceived" to be Samuel, who told him that Israel would be delivered to the Philistines and "to morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me"; Chronicles says Saul died for "asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit".

Later Scripture sets him beside Moses: "Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among them that call upon his name"; "Though Moses and Samuel stood before me". Peter counts "all the prophets from Samuel"; Paul says God gave judges "until Samuel the prophet".

tradition.text: Jerome, writing in his own day, asks whether "the Emperor Arcadius" was guilty of sacrilege, "who after so long a time has conveyed the bones of the blessed Samuel from Judea to Thrace", with crowds meeting the relics "from Palestine to Chalcedon".

questions.question: At Endor, was it Samuel who spoke to Saul?

views.label: Yes, Samuel himself
views.holders: The ancient Jewish church (the Greek of 1 Chronicles 10:13, Ecclesiasticus 46:20, Josephus); Justin, Origen and Augustine; Kirkpatrick (1884), who reports these

argument.text: Kirkpatrick holds that "the spirit of Samuel himself appeared" and calls this "the plain and natural meaning of the narrative": verses 15, 16 and 20 say "Samuel said" and speak of "the words of Samuel". He holds it was God, not the woman, who sent him.

views.label: A spirit taking Samuel’s form
views.holders: Tertullian (about AD 200); followed by Jerome, Luther and Calvin, as reported by Kirkpatrick (1884)

argument.text: Tertullian writes that the spirit consulted at Endor was "permitted ... to represent the soul of Samuel", and "God forbid, however, that we should suppose that the soul of any saint, much less of a prophet, can be dragged out of (its resting-place in Hades) by a demon."

views.label: The woman deceived herself
views.holders: "A modern hypothesis", as reported by Kirkpatrick (1884)

argument.text: Kirkpatrick reports a view that the woman, in a trance, imagined she saw and heard Samuel. He answers that the dialogue runs "directly" between Saul and Samuel.

views.label: A deliberate deception by the woman

argument.text: Kirkpatrick reports a view that the woman pretended to see Samuel and used her own voice or a confederate’s. He says it "finds no support in the narrative".

questions.question: How old was Samuel when the LORD called him?

argument.text: 1 Samuel says "the child Samuel ministered unto the LORD" and that Eli "perceived that the LORD had called the child", but gives no age.
Josephus, retelling Samuel, writes, "Now when Samuel was twelve years old, he began to prophesy".

questions.question: Did Samuel write the books that bear his name?

views.label: Samuel himself wrote it
views.holders: "A late Jewish tradition", as reported by Kirkpatrick (1884)

argument.text: Kirkpatrick reports a late Jewish tradition that ascribes the authorship to Samuel himself. He notes that this "could only apply to the first twenty-four chapters of the First Book", since Samuel’s death is told in chapter 25, and thinks it improbable that even these came from Samuel’s pen in their present form.

views.label: A later compiler drew on prophets’ records

argument.text: Kirkpatrick says "no answer can be given" to who wrote the book; it is "generally agreed" to be a compilation. He holds that its chief sources were "probably contemporary prophetical histories", among them the records of Samuel, Nathan and Gad named in 1 Chronicles 29:29, and that these prophets were "themselves the historians of the period". He notes that others have held the three were the subjects, not the authors, of those works.

notSaid: Scripture gives no age for Samuel at his call.
1 Samuel 28:19 says "to morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me", and 1 Samuel 31:6 tells of Saul’s death with three sons; the text does not say there that the word came to pass.
The book named after Samuel does not say who wrote it; Scripture names one writing of his (1 Samuel 10:25) and "the book of Samuel the seer" (1 Chronicles 29:29).
